summary: Describes RSA and DSA key and signature encoding, and binary key encoding, for version 2 of the KeyNote trust-management system. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: This says exactly how to write down keys and signatures so every KeyNote program reads them the same way.

questions: how to encode rsa and dsa keys for keynote
how are dsa keys encoded in keynote
what is the keynote rsa signature format
which algorithm identifiers does rfc 2792 reserve
subtitle: How KeyNote writes down RSA and DSA keys, signatures and binary identifiers so every implementation reads them the same way.

tldr.problem: KeyNote credentials use public keys to name people and programs, but the same key can be written in different ways (for example base64 or hexadecimal), so implementations need one agreed encoding and a way to compare keys.
tldr.mechanism: Keys and signatures are built as ASN1 structures and then written out as hex or base64 text, with a prefix such as dsa-hex: or sig-rsa-sha1-base64: naming the algorithm and the text encoding.
tldr.outcome: Any KeyNote implementation can decode a key or signature and compare keys in a normalized form. This is an informational memo that reserves the algorithm identifiers for IANA.

facts.label: DSA key
facts.value: SEQUENCE of 4 INTEGERs (y, p, q, g)

today: RFC 2792 is an Informational memo from March 2000. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it works alongside RFC 2704, which defines KeyNote.

sections.title: Why Keys Need an Encoding
sections.content:
KeyNote is a trust-management system. Its policies and credentials, called assertions, say which actions the holders of specific public keys may take. A signed assertion is a credential assertion. The KeyNote system itself is defined in RFC 2704, and this memo assumes the reader already knows it.

Because keys identify principals, an implementation must compare them. The same RSA key might appear in base64 in one credential and in hexadecimal in another, so keys are converted to a normalized canonical form before any comparison. An implementation also has to know the internal structure of an encoded key to decode it.

Other identifiers, such as a passphrase or a random nonce, can also name a principal. If they contain characters that cannot appear in a KeyNote string, they need a simple ASCII encoding. Such identifiers cannot sign anything, so no signature encoding is defined for them.
sections.eli5: The same secret can be written in different alphabets. Before two programs compare keys, they first turn them into one standard form so they can tell if they are really the same.

sections.title: Normalized Forms
sections.content:
Comparisons always happen between normalized forms. The RFC defines three:

  • DSA key: four values, the public value y and the p, q and g parameters.
  • RSA key: two values, the public exponent and the modulus.
  • Binary identifier: the identifier's data itself, so comparison is a binary-string comparison.
sections.eli5: Each kind of key has a short list of numbers that really define it. Two keys are the same if those numbers match, however they were written down.

sections.title: Key Encoding
sections.content:
A DSA key is encoded as an ASN1 SEQUENCE of four INTEGER objects: the public value, then p, q and g, in that order. An RSA key is an ASN1 SEQUENCE of two INTEGER objects: the public exponent, then the modulus. (The RFC's RSA text calls the modulus part "of the DSA key", which appears to be a slip.)

For use in credentials, the ASN1 sequence is then ASCII-encoded, for example as hex digits or base64 characters. The key is labelled with an algorithm name of the form dsa-XXX: or rsa-XXX:, where XXX is hex or base64. Other ASCII encodings may be defined in the future.

A binary identifier has no internal encoding and is treated as a sequence of binary digits. It is ASCII-encoded in the same way and labelled binary-XXX:.
sections.eli5: Each key becomes a short list of big numbers, then the list is turned into letters and digits. A label at the front tells you which kind of key it is and which letters were used.

sections.title: Signatures
sections.content:
Both DSA and RSA signatures are computed over the assertion body and the signature algorithm name. The body runs from the start of the first keyword up to and including the newline just before the Signature: keyword. The algorithm name, including its trailing colon (for example sig-dsa-sha1-base64:), is signed too.

  • DSA: an ASN1 SEQUENCE of two INTEGER objects, r then s. Named sig-dsa-XXX-YYY:. Only SHA1 may be used as the hash with DSA.
  • RSA: an ASN1 OCTET STRING holding the signature value. Named sig-rsa-XXX-YYY:. Either MD5 or SHA1 may be used.

In these names XXX is the hash function and YYY is the ASCII encoding, hex or base64. Binary identifiers are not tied to any cryptographic algorithm, so they cannot be used to validate an assertion.
sections.eli5: A signature is like a wax seal over a letter. The label says which seal-making method was used and how the seal is written down in letters and digits.

sections.title: Security and Reserved Identifiers
sections.content:
The security section is short: the security of credentials using these keys depends directly on the strength of the underlying public key algorithms. For the security of KeyNote itself the RFC points to RFC 2704.

Following that RFC, IANA is asked to keep a registry of reserved algorithm identifiers. This memo reserves six for keys and binary identifiers (rsa-hex, rsa-base64, dsa-hex, dsa-base64, binary-hex, binary-base64) and six for signatures (sig-rsa-md5-hex, sig-rsa-md5-base64, sig-rsa-sha1-hex, sig-rsa-sha1-base64, sig-dsa-sha1-hex, sig-dsa-sha1-base64). The double quotes are not part of the identifiers.
sections.eli5: The authors asked for the label names to be written in an official list so nobody uses the same label for something else.
